questions.prompt: Two teams report their work. The first has found a plant that has grown in the Sahara for centuries and that no botanist had ever recorded. The second has built a machine of a kind that had never existed. Which sentence names what each of them did?

options.text: The first team originated a plant; the second team discovered a machine.
The first team invented a plant; the second team discovered a machine.
The first team discovered a plant; the second team invented a machine.
The first team discovered a plant; the second team originated a machine.

questions.explanation: To discover is to find something that had previously existed but had been unknown, and the plant has been growing there for centuries; to invent is to make or create something new, which is what building a machine of a kind that never existed amounts to. "The first team invented a plant; the second team discovered a machine." turns the two verbs round and claims the first team created the plant. "The first team discovered a plant; the second team originated a machine." gets the first half right, but originate is kept for beginning a new idea, a new method or a new movement, not for building an object. "The first team originated a plant; the second team discovered a machine." is wrong on both counts at once.

questions.prompt: The prefix that reverses "legal" is "il-", the one that reverses "reversible" is "ir-" and the one that reverses "possible" is "im-". What decides which of the three you write?

options.text: The first letter of the word that follows.
The number of syllables in the word.
Whether the word is an adjective or a verb.
Whether the word came into English from Latin or from Greek.

questions.explanation: These are not three prefixes but one, and it changes shape to match the letter it meets: il- before l, im- before m, p and b, ir- before r, and in- before the rest, which gives illegal, immoral, irregular and incurable. "The number of syllables in the word." plays no part: legal and possible have two syllables each and take different forms. "Whether the word is an adjective or a verb." plays no part either, since all three examples here are adjectives. "Whether the word came into English from Latin or from Greek." invents a test the book never applies; what the spelling rule does not tell you is which words take this prefix at all, and that has to be learnt word by word.

questions.prompt: Your module dates four things: the discovery of penicillin, the first man-made satellite orbiting the moon, the invention of the DVD and the invention of disposable contact lenses. Which of them came first?

options.text: the invention of the DVD
disposable contact lenses
the first man-made satellite orbiting the moon
the discovery of penicillin

questions.explanation: Your book dates the discovery of penicillin by the Scottish biologist Alexander Fleming to 1928, which is the earliest of the four by a wide margin. "the first man-made satellite orbiting the moon" is dated 1968, forty years later. "disposable contact lenses" are dated 1987. "the invention of the DVD" is dated 1995 and is in fact the most recent of the four, so it is the exact opposite of the answer. The order to remember is penicillin, then the satellite, then the lenses, then the DVD.

questions.prompt: A science page describes "a sugar-free drink". Which of these phrases is built on exactly the same pattern?

options.text: a widely-respected scientist
a smoke-free hospital
a heat-producing engine
a two-hour test

questions.explanation: sugar-free is a noun followed by an adjective, the pattern your grammar summary illustrates with odour-free tablets, and "a smoke-free hospital" repeats it exactly: a noun, then the adjective free. "a widely-respected scientist" is an adverb followed by a past participle, the pattern of genetically-modified. "a heat-producing engine" is a noun followed by an -ing form, the pattern of life-threatening. "a two-hour test" is a number followed by a noun, the pattern of 24-hour shopping. All four are correctly built compound adjectives; only one of them is built the same way as the phrase in the question.

questions.prompt: One of your book's captions reads: "Technology is good but it mustn't fall in the wrong hands." A pupil rewrites it as: "Technology is good but it needn't fall in the wrong hands." What has the change done?

options.text: It has turned a ban into the statement that there is no necessity.
It has turned a ban into a much stronger ban.
It has turned a ban into a piece of friendly advice about storing equipment safely.
It has left the meaning of the caption exactly as it was.

questions.explanation: mustn't forbids: the caption says that letting technology fall into the wrong hands is not allowed. needn't states the absence of necessity, so the new sentence says only that nothing obliges technology to fall into the wrong hands, and it forbids nothing at all. "It has turned a ban into a much stronger ban." reads needn't as an intensified must, which it never is. "It has turned a ban into a piece of friendly advice about storing equipment safely." describes what should would have done. "It has left the meaning of the caption exactly as it was." is the most expensive of the four mistakes: mustn't and needn't sit at opposite ends of the scale, one closing a door and the other leaving it open.
